prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

No remembering now when the apple sapling was blown almost out of the ground. No telling how, with all the other trees around, it alone was struck. It must have been luck, he thought for years, so close to the house it grew. It must have been night. Change is a thing one sleeps through when young, and he was young. If there was a weakness in the earth, a give he went down on his knees to find and feel the limits of, there is no longer. If there was one random blow from above the way he's come to know from years in this place, the roots were stronger. Whatever the case, he has watched this tree survive wind ripping at his roof for nights on end, heats and blights that left little else alive. No remembering now... A day's changes mean all to him and all days come down to one clear pane through which he sees among all the other trees this leaning, clenched, unyielding one that seems cast in the form of a blast that would have killed it, as if something at the heart of things, and with the heart of things, had willed it.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker cannot remember when or why the apple sapling was nearly uprooted while the surrounding trees were spared.
- He once attributed the tree’s survival to luck, its proximity to the house, or the strength of its roots.
- Over the years, he has watched the tree endure fierce winds, extreme heat, and blight that destroyed much of the life around it.
- The tree remains permanently bent yet unyielding, shaped by the force that nearly killed it.
- To the speaker, the tree’s survival suggests a deeper will or purpose at the heart of existence.
prompts.L4:

An aging observer reflects on an apple tree nearly uprooted in his youth, using its endurance through storms, heat, and blight to contemplate change and survival. The tree’s permanent lean embodies resistance to destruction, suggesting a profound inner will that transforms trauma into resilience.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Change, Whatever

outputs.L1:
He cannot remember now when the apple sapling was blown almost out of the ground. Nor can he say why, with all the other trees around it, this one alone was struck. For years he thought it must have been luck, growing as it did so close to the house. It must have happened at night. Change is something one sleeps through when young, and he was young. If there was a weakness in the earth, some yielding place whose limits he went down on his knees to find and feel, it is there no longer. If there was one random blow from above, the kind he has come to know through his years in this place, the roots proved stronger.

Whatever the case, he has watched this tree survive winds that tore at his roof for nights on end, heats and blights that left little else alive. He cannot remember now. A day’s changes mean everything to him, and all his days resolve into a single clear pane through which, among all the other trees, he sees this leaning, clenched, unyielding one, seemingly cast in the shape of the blast that would have killed it—as if something at the heart of things, and with the heart of things, had willed it.
outputs.L2:
He can no longer recall the moment the young apple tree was nearly torn from the soil, nor explain why it was the only one hit among all the surrounding trees. For years he assumed chance had spared it, growing as it did beside the house. The storm must have come after dark. He was young then, and youth can sleep through transformation. Perhaps the ground had once been soft or fractured—some yielding place he knelt to examine and trace—but any such flaw is gone now. Or perhaps it suffered one of the sudden strikes from the sky that his long years here have taught him to recognize, only to find its roots equal to the force.

Whatever happened, he has since seen the tree endure winds that clawed at the roof for nights without stopping, along with heat and disease that killed almost everything else. The memory itself has vanished. Now, each day’s smallest alteration matters to him, and every day narrows into a single transparent view: amid all the trees stands this bent, tight-fisted, immovable survivor, shaped as though permanently molded by the very explosion that should have destroyed it—as if a will within the core of existence, acting together with that core, had commanded it to live.
outputs.L3:
The speaker can no longer remember exactly when the apple sapling was nearly torn from the ground, nor why it alone was struck while the surrounding trees remained unharmed. At first, he explained its survival in ordinary terms: perhaps it had simply been lucky, perhaps the shelter of the nearby house had protected it, or perhaps its young roots were stronger than they appeared.

As the years passed, however, he watched the tree withstand trial after trial. Fierce winds battered its branches, relentless heat scorched the land, and blight destroyed much of the life growing around it. Still, the apple tree endured. It never fully recovered its original shape; the force that had almost uprooted it left it permanently bent. Yet that bent form became a sign not of defeat, but of resilience. Marked by what nearly killed it, the tree continues to stand, damaged but unyielding.

To the speaker, its survival can no longer be explained by chance alone. The tree seems to embody a deeper will—a mysterious purpose or determination at the heart of existence itself. Its persistence suggests that life contains an instinct to endure, even when it is wounded, altered, and tested almost beyond its limits.
outputs.L4:
When I was young, a violent autumn storm nearly tore the apple tree from the earth. By morning, half its roots lay exposed, dark and tangled in the wet grass, and the trunk leaned so sharply that everyone believed it would soon fall. Yet my father pressed the loosened soil back around its base and bound the tree with rope. For a season it stood supported by stakes, trembling whenever the wind returned.

The ropes and stakes are long gone. So are the hands that fastened them. I have grown old beneath the tree’s crooked branches, watching it endure winter gales, summers of fierce heat, and years when blight blackened its leaves and spoiled its fruit. Time has hollowed parts of the trunk, and several limbs have broken under snow, but each spring a scatter of blossoms still appears. Some years the harvest is meager; in others, the boughs bend beneath small, sharp-scented apples.

The tree never straightened. Its wound became its shape. Even now it leans toward the field as if the old storm were still passing through it. But what once seemed a sign of defeat has become proof of endurance. The roots that remained took firmer hold, and the surviving branches learned to grow toward the light from their altered position.

Looking at it, I think of all that changes us without destroying us. We do not return to what we were before loss, illness, fear, or age. We carry these forces in our posture, in our silences, in the paths our lives take afterward. Survival is not the restoration of an untouched form. It is the difficult art of continuing in another shape.

Perhaps the tree knows nothing of courage. Perhaps its persistence is only the blind labor of sap, root, and leaf. Yet I cannot stand beneath it without sensing some inward refusal—a will buried deeper than the storm could reach. The wind altered it, but did not claim it. The years diminished it, but did not empty it of life. Still leaning, still scarred, it blossoms.
outputs.L5:
**Change, Whatever**

Change rarely asks for permission. It enters quietly through a new habit, an unexpected goodbye, or a decision made on an ordinary afternoon. Sometimes we welcome it; sometimes we resist with everything we have.

“Whatever,” we say, pretending not to care. Yet the word can hide disappointment, fear, or even hope. It can mean surrender—but it can also mean freedom: whatever happens, I will adapt; whatever comes, I will keep moving.

Change reminds us that nothing remains fixed forever. We lose familiar paths, but discover new directions. We leave behind old versions of ourselves and become someone we could not have imagined.

So, whatever the future brings, change will be part of it. The challenge is not to control every outcome, but to meet it with courage, curiosity, and the willingness to begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about an old man reflecting on an apple tree that was nearly uprooted when he was young but survived and grew permanently bent by the wind.
counterfactuals.output:
The apple tree has leaned toward the east for seventy years, as if listening for something buried beyond the hill. I remember the night the wind nearly took it. I was a boy then, awake beneath the rafters while the whole house groaned like a ship. At dawn, its roots were lifted from the earth, pale and tangled, clutching clods of rain-dark soil. My father pressed them back with his boots. We tied the trunk with rope and prayed in the practical way of farmers: with stakes, mud, and our shoulders.

It lived, though it never stood straight again.

Each spring it flowered at an angle, spilling white blossoms into the grass. Each autumn its apples hung like small red lanterns along the bowed branches. Children climbed it more easily because of its wound. Birds nested in the crook the storm had made. Even the bees seemed to love its crookedness, their gold bodies moving among the blooms as if gathering sweetness from an old sorrow.

Now I am older than my father was that morning. My hands have become his hands—knotted, brown-spotted, slow. I sit beneath the tree and feel its shadow lying slantwise over me. The wind moves through it, and the leaves turn their silver undersides, whispering of that night, of the roots exposed, of the earth opening and closing again.

There are lives that rise like steeples, and lives that bend toward the ground. Yet here we are, the tree and I, neither of us what we might have been, both shaped by weather we could not refuse. It bears less fruit now. I remember less. But sometimes an apple falls beside me with a soft, final thud, and when I lift it, its skin is cool and fragrant, and I think: the wind did not win. It only gave the tree another way to stand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single literary paragraph in a meditative, rural style, using a storm-damaged sapling as a symbol of resilience, memory, aging, and fate.
counterfactuals.output: At the edge of the field, where the stone wall sank beneath nettles and last year’s leaves, a young ash leaned from the wound the storm had given it, its thin trunk split but not severed, one green branch lifting toward the rinsed and indifferent sky. Each morning the old farmer paused beside it, remembering trees now gone—the orchard of his boyhood, the elm beneath which his father had sharpened scythes—and he saw how time did not heal so much as teach the broken where to grow. The sapling’s scar would widen with its rings, carried inward even as bark closed over it, just as his own years held their vanished faces and unfinished words. Whether the tree would stand for fifty winters or fall in the next hard wind was no more his to know than the hour appointed for himself; yet there it was, fastening its roots deeper into the dark, accepting both rain and ruin, and making from the shape of its injury a new way to reach the light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a man looking through his window at a leaning apple tree that has endured decades of storms, drought, and blight. Make the tree seem shaped by the very force that almost killed it.
counterfactuals.output:
He stood at the kitchen window, one hand resting on the sill, and watched the old apple tree lean into the field. Decades of wind had worried it eastward, twisting its trunk until the grain seemed to flow like frozen water. Drought had split its bark; blight had blackened limbs that still reached among the living ones like charred fingers. Each storm had taken something—branches, blossoms, whole seasons of fruit—yet the tree had grown around every wound. Knuckles of new wood sealed the breaks. Roots rose from the earth like ropes pulled tight. Even its few apples hung on the sheltered side, small and bright.

It no longer looked like a tree resisting the weather. It looked like weather made solid: bent, scarred, and still bearing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective passage that begins and ends with “No remembering now,” avoids dialogue, and explores how childhood changes blur together while one damaged tree remains a vivid emblem of survival.
counterfactuals.output:
No remembering now, only the soft collapse of years into one another: classrooms changing their smells, shoes growing tight, faces lengthening in photographs, summers losing their vastness. Childhood did not end in a single moment. It thinned like mist, each change too small to notice until the whole landscape had altered.

Yet the tree remains. Lightning had split its trunk before memory properly began, leaving one side blackened and hollow. Still, every spring, leaves gathered on its surviving branches. I measured myself against that scar, mistaking endurance for stillness. Now I understand that survival was not the refusal to change, but the stubborn making of green from what remained.

Everything else blurs—the rooms, the seasons, the child I was—but that wounded tree stands clear, rooted in the vanished yard, holding ruin and renewal in the same body. I return to it without returning, carrying its image where certainty used to be, and let the years close over me.

No remembering now,
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create poetic fiction about a farmer who cannot recall the night an apple sapling was almost torn from the earth, but who has watched it outlive other trees and come to believe that something at the heart of existence willed it to endure.
counterfactuals.output:
The old farmer could remember the birth of every tree in the north orchard except one.

He remembered planting the pears in a silver rain, his wife laughing as mud climbed past the buckles of her shoes. He remembered the row of cherries his brother brought from the coast, their roots wrapped in sailcloth and smelling faintly of salt. He remembered the lightning year, when the tallest elm opened like a black flower and burned until morning.

But of the apple sapling beside the stone wall—of the night it was almost torn from the earth—he remembered nothing.

Others told him the storm had been terrible.

They said the wind came down from the hills with the voices of wolves. It lifted shingles, overturned the water trough, and rolled the empty hay cart into the river. At dawn they found the young apple bent flat beneath the wall, three roots torn loose and pale as knucklebones.

They found the farmer there, too, barefoot in the mud.

His nightshirt was ripped. His palms were bleeding. A length of rope ran from the sapling’s narrow trunk to his own waist, knotted so tightly it had to be cut away.

He had no memory of tying it.

All he knew was that he woke in his bed with earth under his nails and the taste of rain in his mouth.

The neighbors said he must have gone out in his sleep. His wife said fear had emptied the night from him. The doctor tapped the farmer’s skull and spoke of shock, exhaustion, the merciful tricks of the mind.

The farmer accepted every explanation and believed none of them.

He reset the roots and packed the soil with both hands. The sapling leaned east after that, as though listening forever to the departing storm. No one expected fruit from it. For years it gave only a handful of small, bitter apples, green even when autumn reddened the hills.

Yet it lived.

It lived when blight passed through the orchard and darkened the pear leaves. It lived when ice broke the cherries one by one, their beautiful limbs scattered over the snow. It lived through the summer the well failed and the grass became tinder. His wife died in winter. His brother followed in spring. The elm stump softened, filled with beetles, and sank slowly into the ground.

Still the apple tree flowered.

Its blossoms were neither brighter nor more fragrant than others. Its trunk was twisted. One limb dragged so low that foxes brushed against it as they crossed the field. But each April, the farmer would wake to find the tree clothed in white, as if the night had remembered how to make stars and had hung them there.

In old age, he sat beneath it with his back against the scar where the rope had once bitten through the bark.

He tried to summon that lost night.

Sometimes he imagined the storm had spoken his name. Sometimes he thought the tree itself had cried out—not in any sound the ear could catch, but in the deep speech by which roots call to rain and seeds bargain with darkness.

Perhaps, he thought, he had not saved it.

Perhaps they had both been held.

By what, he could not say. He had long ago ceased to picture heaven as a throne above the clouds. What he believed in now was nearer and stranger: a pulse hidden inside ruined things, a will without face or voice, moving through root and blood alike. Something at the heart of existence that did not promise safety, did not forbid suffering, but sometimes, for reasons beyond love or deserving, said:

*This one. Let this one remain.*

One autumn evening, the farmer picked the last apple.

The orchard around him was mostly meadow now. Goldenrod stood where the pears had grown. Mice nested beneath the old cherry mounds. Beyond the wall, the hills darkened under a sky the color of worn iron.

He turned the apple in his hands. It was small and misshapen, flushed red on only one side. When he bit into it, the flesh was sweet.

Not very sweet. Not miraculously sweet.

Sweet enough.

The farmer closed his eyes. Wind moved through the crooked branches above him, and for one instant he felt a rope around his waist, rain against his face, the whole black earth straining to keep what it had made.

Then the feeling vanished.

The tree bent over him, listening east.

And beneath them both, in the deep country where memory could not go, the roots held fast.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
